response.message: We're building an Azure predictive-maintenance flow. Synthetic sensor histories and maintenance records feed Azure ML feature preparation, a versioned model with a time-based held-out test, drift monitoring and a work-order draft that an operator reviews. The system never controls equipment. In the first local test, the fixtures exercise the data flow with a scripted (mocked) model, so it tests the wiring but not prediction quality; real validation needs a trained model scored on held-out data from a later time period. For the labels: what should count as "maintenance needed", for example a recorded failure or an unplanned repair, and how far ahead should we warn, for example 7 days?

proposal.title: Azure predictive-maintenance end-to-end sketch
proposal.body: Scope: ingesting synthetic sensor and maintenance-record data, feature preparation, a time-split training run with held-out evaluation, a versioned registry, batch scoring, drift monitoring and an operator-approved work-order draft. Equipment control is excluded. Assumptions: Azure services are named for intent only. Region, account access, quotas and interoperability are not verified, and nothing is deployed. Native Terraform for these Azure ML services is not generated yet and needs engineering. Local test: fixtures run the flow with a scripted model. This proves the wiring, not model quality.

requirementDrafts.rationale: If equipment were triggered automatically, a wrong prediction could cause physical harm or downtime.
requirementDrafts.basis: User: "No automatic equipment control" and "an operator work-order draft".
requirementDrafts.statement: Proposed: predictions only create draft work orders that an operator approves. The system never sends commands to equipment.

requirementDrafts.rationale: A random split leaks future information and overstates accuracy. The false-alarm rate drives operator trust.
requirementDrafts.statement: Proposed: before a model version is registered for use, it is evaluated on held-out data from a later time period than the training data. The acceptance thresholds are still to be agreed.

requirementDrafts.rationale: Sensor behaviour changes over time, and silent drift degrades the warnings.
requirementDrafts.statement: Proposed: monitor input and prediction drift against the registered model's baseline and alert the model owner when drift is detected. The thresholds are still to be agreed.

Do not just recite a checklist or demand that a junior developer repair product internals. Offer a concrete supported correction when possible; otherwise ask one focused question and explain why its answer matters. Help improve this architecture from its current emulation results. Preserve all required components, existing systems, IDs, established service choices, access boundaries and requirements. response.message:
The good news first: the emulation report shows no failures, and the whole flow is still connected end to end. That runs from sensors and records through Event Hubs, the data lake, Azure ML features, training, the registry and batch scoring to the drift monitor and the operator's draft work orders. The status is "blocked" because none of the 8 Azure ML pipeline blocks has a native generator yet, so the emulator had nothing to run. That's product engineering work, not a mistake in our design. A reproducer would be design revision 2 with artifact 54a49401…, which fails the first gap, "Event Hubs ingestion: Implementation needed".

None of the supported contracts fits this workload. Azure private object storage would only cover the data lake, and that would shrink the app to storage, which you've ruled out. So I haven't changed the board, and nothing has been validated or deployed yet.

Even before that engineering work lands, we can settle one decision. The first block, "Synthetic sensor histories: Existing — reference/import plan needed", needs to know how that existing data reaches us. How should the synthetic data get in? For example, a script could replay sensor events into Event Hubs, or we could load files straight into the data lake.
